text:
And he thought of putting out the light in the room so as to have more courage,
but he wished for a glimmer to filter in, a half-light growing gradually more
discernible, perhaps from the streetlamps in the road, perhaps from a shaded
lamp in the adjoining room. And he smelled the fragrance of her body diffused
about him, that same fragrance, but sweeter, which he had had upon his mouth
when kissing her; an intense and manifold fragrance that blossomed from her
skin, as though roses were hidden in the folds of her body. He savored the
freshness of that springtime flesh, imagined caressing her round bare shoulder,
slipped his groping hand into the velvety warmth of her armpits, gathered her
torso, pliant as a young shoot, into his tight embrace, felt against himself the
unrestrainable throbbing of her womb, the way her body would entwine itself with
his body, to offer itself and to defend itself, conceived the savage joy of
being able to stun her, heard in her throat the death rattle of fleeing
virginity, heard her weep in rapture, laugh in pain... then he saw her as she
was, slender, arched, strong in her slightness, grow pale for a moment with that
pallor which is near to death, and flash forth in all her beauty with love amid
that exultant hatred with which the virgin gives herself...

But suddenly she had felt ill. Truly, just as in his vision, he had seen her
turn white with that same pallor, had felt his arms seized by her convulsed
hands, then, seeing her stagger, had supported her against himself.

“What is it, Lora?”

She did not answer; her teeth were chattering; she was trembling.

“Lora! Lora! What is it?”

“Nothing...” she stammered, “it will pass...”

It was only a dizzy spell, and soon her mouth smiled at him again. They resumed
their journey; he supported her as far as the carriage.

The coachman prattled; the little horse began trotting again toward the city of
its martyrdom, where there were the rough paving stone, the slippery rail, the
posting station, and the stable. On either side of the two hedges, fragrant in
the white night, the tilled earth was growing grains and fruits for the
voracious city; some cricket in love with the moon raised its shrill song,
infinitely greater than itself.

Now her head hurt; around her temples she had an iron band that hammered. To
soothe that pain she took one of her brother’s hands and wrapped it around her
forehead.

“Are you suffering?”

“Yes, a little.”

He encircled her forehead, from one temple to the other, with countless little
kisses.

“Keep me close, very close... and I shall recover.”

In a garden they passed, the May roses were opening their calyxes swollen with
spring.

“Do you still feel ill?”

“Yes, a sweet pain...”

Beyond a row of poplars, the city’s red blaze reappeared like a vast cloud
suspended in the firmament. They reached the first houses, with walls white in
the moonlight. Now the crickets were a hundred, were a thousand, lost in the
May hay, and one, more wrathful than all the others, seemed to pursue them close
behind along the hawthorn hedge.

Suddenly she let her head fall back against his shoulder, as though the onset
of a faint were overcoming her.

“Rigo, I feel ill...” she stammered, pressing her breast.

“But what is it?” he said, distraught. “Why are you suffering so?”

She closed her eyes and tried once more to smile at him from her wholly white
face.

“I feel dizzy... I don’t know...”

“Do you want to stop? What do you want to do?”

“Nothing; it will pass now... it will pass... I love you...”

When they reached the last farmhouse, the cricket’s wandering song faded far
away, infinitely far away, and died. But before them appeared the monumental
tollhouse, majestic as a triumphal arch beneath the starry sky. The customs
guards, seated near the booth, laughed and smoked, chatting with women of ill
repute. Amid throngs of children, several vagrants were playing a peddler’s
raffle game; an eater of flaming tow gaped his enormous soot-blackened mouth
before the astonished spectators.

“I love you...” she said again, in a breath, to her pale lover.

And the hair shirt of unconsumable guilt clothed their desperate flesh like a
mantle of thorns.




VIII


He arrived unexpectedly at Clara Michelis’s house around lunchtime. She had
not seen him for several days; she had written to him several times without
receiving an answer, and had repeatedly gone to his house, but had never found
him there. She could not regard Arrigo’s neglecting her as unusual; yet he had
never shown himself indifferent to such a degree.

Mother and daughter were sitting at the table when he arrived. The servant was
the first to ask him whether he had already eaten lunch.

After he answered no, his customary place was laid for him, and he sat down
there with the air of a broken man.

“I have had a great deal to do these past few days,” he said by way of apology.
“Forgive me for not coming.”

Neither the daughter nor the servants were any longer surprised by his presence
in that house; he had become something of its master, everyone knew in what
capacity, and by now no one paid any further attention to it. That day his face
was pale and agitated, his eyes full of fever, his hands somewhat restless.

“I have been extremely busy,” he repeated, as though he did not know what else
to say.

Out of regard for her daughter, Clara did not say a word, but remained looking
at him, staring at him, with her gentle eyes full of tenderness and
resignation. She was greatly afraid of him when she saw him arrive in that
state. She too looked worn, and because she had expected to be alone, she had
come to lunch in a dressing gown without having finished making herself
presentable. Face powder left a visible trace upon her somewhat worn skin; her
neck, emerging slenderly from the lace around the low neckline, had the
appearance of something diseased; as she ate, a few very slight wrinkles formed
at the corners of her mouth and near the arches of her eyebrows. Perhaps she
had wept during the sleepless night; her eyes seemed to have grown dim, and
they turned toward her lover a gaze full of anguished tenderness.

Adelina, by contrast, appeared wholly fresh in her blooming seventeen years;
but that Signor Arrigo made her a little uncomfortable when, instead of joking
with her as usual, he came with that mastiff’s face of his and from time to time
looked at her with eyes as fierce as those of some great nocturnal bird.

“What ever have you had to do all these days?” Clara finally asked, trying to
give her words a playful tone.

“Many things,” he said. “I shall tell you.”

And at once, to change the subject, he turned to the young lady:

“And you, Lela, how are you?” He tried to smile, but his face was tense.

“Lela is very well,” the girl replied merrily. “It seems to me, though, that
you are not very well.”

“Why?”

“Why, did you not look at yourself in the mirror this morning?”

“Ah... I had no time to shave: that is the reason. And then my head hurts a
little.”

“And you are not eating?”

“Yes, I am eating; but I have little appetite.”

“Perhaps you would like to take something for your headache?” Clara
interrupted, looking at him with eyes already full of forgiveness.
